line: c4 Nf6 d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Bg2 O-O O-O
teaches: A setup that stays popular for decades usually earned it structurally, not fashionably — when one scheme answers several defences at once, that consistency IS the argument for it.
explains: Both kings are tucked away and the bishop sits home on g2 on the long diagonal. This whole scheme is built around that bishop — one setup that answers a dozen defences — and that consistency is exactly why it has been among White's best tries for decades. Black has a real menu of replies from here, and none of them is refuted; they are simply different games.

line: c4 Nf6 d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Bg2 O-O O-O Nbd7
teaches: Between two developing squares for the same knight, prefer the one the opponent's pawn break cannot hit — denying a tempo is worth more than the extra square the other move covers.
explains: Two squares for this knight, and the difference is a whole tempo. On c6 it would stand right in front of White's d-pawn, so the push to d5 arrives hitting it and White gains time — so we choose d7 instead, where that same advance hits nothing. The knight still does its real job from here: it guards e5 and readies the central pawn strike the whole setup is built around. The oldest and easiest of these systems to learn, and a thoroughly practical way to play it.

line: c4 Nf6 d4 g6 g3 Bg7 Nf3 d6 Bg2 O-O O-O Nbd7 Bg5 Nb8 Bc1
teaches: Before pinning, check whether the capture would actually win something — a pin against a defended piece threatens nothing, so the opponent can simply ask the bishop where it means to live.
explains: The bishop went out to g5 to pin, and has come straight back to c1. It is a club favourite and it is a mistake: the knight it pinned was defended, so taking on f6 won nothing — which means the bishop only committed itself to a square a pawn can kick for free. Two moves spent, nothing gained, and it is the same position with Black to move.
